source: Slobin (1996) From 'thought and language' to 'thinking for speaking'
finding: Founding statement. Learning a first language trains a child to attend, while speaking, to the kinds of event features that the language grammaticalises. This 'thinking for speaking' is a thinking mode that applies only while a message is being encoded for speech.
numbers: Chapter in Gumperz & Levinson (eds) Rethinking Linguistic Relativity, pp. 70-96. Page-76 claim (as quoted by others): a child learns particular ways of thinking for speaking.
limits: PhilArchive and PhilPapers copies returned 403 this session; known only from secondary descriptions (search summaries, Papafragou 2008, Wikipedia). Not read.
agent_relevance: The claim is narrow: language shapes what is selected when writing a message, not what the speaker can perceive or remember. For an LLM that only emits text, this narrow claim is the relevant one.

source: Wikipedia: Linguistic relativity (History section)
finding: Wikipedia describes Slobin's thinking for speaking as the translation of perceptual and prelinguistic cognition into linguistic terms for communication, and as the process underlying relativity. It cites Bowerman as showing that early spatial reasoning and categorisation develop largely independently of language.
numbers: One paragraph, footnotes 65-66; the Slobin sentence carries a 'clarification needed' tag.
limits: Tertiary source, no numbers; only the first 100k of 189k characters were read.
agent_relevance: Background only. Shows the weak, domain-specific reading is the mainstream summary.

source: Papafragou, Hulbert & Trueswell (2008) Does language guide event perception? Evidence from eye movements
finding: Core test of thinking for speaking with eye tracking. English and Greek speakers watched 3-second animated motion events and either described them (Linguistic task) or studied them for a memory test (Nonlinguistic task). Gaze differed by language only when speakers were preparing to talk, and only for bounded events where the verb typology differs.
numbers: N=17 English + 17 Greek (3 more dropped for track loss). 12 clip-art animations, 3 s motion then 2 s frozen frame. Bounded events: manner verbs 72% English vs 36% Greek; unbounded 76% vs 54%. Path verbs in bounded events: 16% English vs 39% Greek.
quote: attention allocation during event perception is not affected by the perceiver's native language
limits: Small samples (17 per group); instrumental manner events with clip-art agents only; one language pair.
agent_relevance: Language effects on attention appear when a message is being planned and vanish in free inspection. Suggests output-format wording steers what the model selects, not what it can represent.

source: Papafragou, Hulbert & Trueswell (2008) Does language guide event perception? Evidence from eye movements
finding: Time course in the Linguistic task: language-specific looking started in the first second of motion, before any speech. Greek speakers looked at the path endpoint sooner, then at manner; English speakers looked at the endpoint later.
numbers: First second: Language x Region interaction F1(1,16)=4.01, p=.03, partial eta2=.20; F2(1,11)=10.14, p=.004. Third second reversed: F1(1,16)=3.43, p=.04; F2(1,11)=7.40. Median speech latency after the beep 1267 ms (n=13); 88% of trials spoke within 2000 ms.
limits: Modest p-values in 1 s windows; item analyses use only 12 items.
agent_relevance: Planning for output reorders attention within a second. Message planning starts early, not only when writing.

source: Papafragou, Hulbert & Trueswell (2008) Does language guide event perception? Evidence from eye movements
finding: Nonlinguistic task: eye movements were nearly identical across languages while events unfolded. Differences appeared only after the video froze, and in the opposite direction: speakers studied the component their verb does not encode.
numbers: Interaction first reliable in 4th second: F1(1,14)=6.31, p=.01, eta2=.31; 5th second F1(1,14)=9.66, p=.003, eta2=.41. Both groups preferred path endpoints over manner regions overall.
limits: Post-freeze compensation is a language-linked strategy, not a perception difference.
agent_relevance: A model inspecting input with no speaking task should show no language-specific bias. Matches 'language matters when verbalising'.

source: Papafragou, Hulbert & Trueswell (2008) Does language guide event perception? Evidence from eye movements
finding: Memory result: language affected memory only in the Nonlinguistic task, as a cost for Greek speakers who studied both components. Speakers who described the events remembered paths equally well in both languages.
numbers: Path-endpoint memory % correct, bounded/unbounded. Linguistic: English 92/91, Greek 92/92. Nonlinguistic: English 90/88, Greek 73/71. Language x Task F1(1,25)=4.95, p=.01, eta2=.17. 5 participants dropped for a 'same' bias (>=60%).
limits: One cell drives it; not replicated here; 5 exclusions were about 15% of the sample.
agent_relevance: Verbalising fixes which parts are kept. Writing a description can protect or distort memory of what was encoded.

source: Gleitman, January, Nappa & Trueswell (2007) On the give and take between event apprehension and utterance formulation
finding: Attention shapes sentence structure. Capturing gaze on one character makes that character more likely to be the sentence subject and changes verb and word order choice. Early endogenous gaze shifts also change word order.
numbers: Two experiments (perspective predicates, conjoined NPs, actives vs passives, symmetrical predicates). Effect sizes not read.
limits: Only the abstract was seen (retrieval returned metadata and abstract). Static pictures.
agent_relevance: Message structure and attention are coupled both ways. Order of facts shown to a model may shape the order of its description.

source: Bunger, Trueswell & Papafragou (2012) The relation between event apprehension and utterance formulation in children
finding: Adults and 4-year-olds gaze alike while viewing motion events in both tasks, even though children's descriptions omit Manner or Path far more often. So omissions come from the production system, not from different attention during encoding.
numbers: 20 adults + 20 four-year-olds (8 more excluded). Adults mentioned both manner and path in 70% of descriptions, preschoolers in 26%. Mean length 7.7 words adults, 5.8 preschool. Adults mentioned manner in every utterance and path in about two-thirds.
limits: English only, one event type. Slobin's grammar-learning account is not tested directly.
agent_relevance: A gap in output can arise at the writing step while the internal representation is complete. Argues for checking the output step separately from understanding.

source: Bunger, Papafragou & Trueswell (2013) Event structure influences language production: structural priming in motion event description
finding: Priming study showing conceptual event structure is a level that feeds message planning. Prime sentences primed what information speakers include, how it maps to words, and the syntax, but only when primes and targets overlapped conceptually.
numbers: 70 adult English speakers kept (15 excluded), two experiments. With no lexical or conceptual overlap, priming failed.
quote: conceptual structure is a level of representation activated during priming
limits: Effect sizes not extracted; English only.
agent_relevance: Supports a staged pipeline: conceptual message first, linguistic formulation second. Cf. a scaffold that separates what to say from how to say it.

source: Gennari, Sloman, Malt & Fitch (2002) Motion events in language and cognition
finding: Classic early test with English and Spanish speakers. Language differences in describing motion events did not show up in non-verbal similarity or memory tasks; they emerged when verbal encoding was involved.
numbers: No figures read this session.
limits: Not opened (publisher PDF blocked). Summarised from memory and from citations in Papafragou 2008. Unverified here.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as Papafragou 2008: language effects follow verbal encoding.

source: Berman & Slobin (1994) Relating events in narrative: a crosslinguistic developmental study
finding: Frog-story method: children and adults in several languages narrate the same picture book. Narratives differ by language in what is encoded (manner, path, temporal and aspectual marking, scene setting). Source data of the thinking-for-speaking claim.
numbers: Not read; numbers not recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: A ready paradigm for comparing LLM narration across languages.

source: Talmy (1985; 2000) Lexicalization patterns; Toward a Cognitive Semantics
finding: Typology behind the studies. Satellite-framed languages (English) put manner in the verb and path in a satellite; verb-framed languages (Greek, Spanish) put path in the verb and add manner optionally.
limits: Not opened; known through citation in Papafragou 2008.
agent_relevance: Gives the typological variable on which LLM studies could be stratified.

source: Levelt (1989) Speaking; Griffin & Bock (2000) What the eyes say about speaking
finding: Standard production model: conceptualisation (macro and micro planning) yields a preverbal message, then formulation, then articulation. Griffin and Bock showed gaze reaches a described object before the word, with static pictures. Thinking for speaking is the micro-planning stage inside this model.
numbers: Figures not read.
limits: Not opened; cited in Papafragou 2008 as precedent for early gaze effects.
agent_relevance: The main formal production model. A scaffold that plans a message before drafting copies this structure.

source: Isasi-Isasmendi et al. (2023) The agent preference in visual event apprehension
finding: Brief-exposure (300 ms) study across a case-marking-agents language (Basque, ergative) and Spanish. Agents got more attention and recognition in both languages and tasks. Language modulated it: Basque speakers were more accurate on agent probes and less accurate on patient probes than Spanish speakers.
numbers: Experiment 1 online: Basque N=90, Spanish N=88. Two tasks (description, probe questions). Bayesian regression. No language effect on agent description specificity; Basque speakers were more specific describing patients.
limits: Language effects were not consistent across tasks; authors note typing time and memory decay may blur description results.
agent_relevance: Language-specific effects can appear in recognition, but small and task-dependent. Evidence for the weak form.

source: Montero-Melis (2021) Consistency in motion event encoding across languages
finding: Swedish (satellite-framed) speakers encoded almost all caused-motion events with one syntactic frame and nearly always gave manner. Spanish speakers varied much more, and the variability came from the speaker more than from the event.
numbers: N=84 Spanish and Swedish speakers; 32 caused-motion events. Swedish descriptions substantially more consistent than Spanish. Exact statistics not extracted.
limits: Production only; no cognition measure.
agent_relevance: Language bias strength differs by language, and speaker habit outweighs event properties. In an LLM, habit corresponds to prompt and decoding habit.

source: Lee, Unal & Papafragou (2026) Event segmentation in language and cognition
finding: English and Turkish speakers. Robust language differences in linguistic event units (Exp 1) but no difference in a classic non-linguistic event segmentation task (Exp 2) or an event enumeration task (Exp 3). Conceptual and linguistic event units are related but distinct.
numbers: Exp 1: 39 English and 42 Turkish speakers, 30 videos of 2500 ms, Simple Path vs Source/Goal Path groups. Exp 3: proportion of 2-event responses not different by language (beta=-0.10, SE 0.43, z=-0.22, p=.82); Source/Goal path gave more 2-event answers in both languages (beta=-1.83, z=-3.03, p=.002); no interaction (p=.73).
quote: conceptual and linguistic event units are related but distinct levels of event structure
limits: Two languages. Null effects are not proof of equality.
agent_relevance: Another failure to find a language effect on non-linguistic cognition while output units differ.

source: Chen, Papafragou & Trueswell (2026) The Goal bias emerges during motion event perception and affects language production and memory
finding: Goals are attended over Sources during initial event encoding. The bias is stronger in free inspection than when preparing a description. The size of the bias predicts whether the Source is later mentioned or remembered.
numbers: 128 native American English speakers; 28 clips of 5 s, 16 critical (Figure moves from Source to Goal); eye tracking while viewing or preparing to describe, then memory test.
limits: English only. Correlational link between gaze and later mention.
agent_relevance: A language-independent bias that speech planning weakens. Planning to speak can change a default attentional bias.

source: Unal, Wilson, Trueswell & Papafragou (2024) Asymmetries in encoding event roles: evidence from language and cognition
finding: Four experiments: event-role prominence in language and in non-linguistic tasks is similar but not identical. Patients are more salient than Goals, which are more salient than Instruments, in both. Agents beat Patients in descriptions and visual search but not in change detection.
numbers: Four experiments (description, visual search, change blindness). Per-experiment sample sizes not extracted. Cites work showing event roles can be recognised from displays as short as 37 ms.
limits: Abstract and introduction read; no per-experiment numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Prominence in wording overlaps with, but is not the same as, prominence in cognition, so wording is not a clean readout of what the agent represents.

source: Coco, Fernandes, Arai & Keller (2026) Cross-linguistic coordination of overt attention and speech production as evidence for a language of vision
finding: Eye movements and descriptions in English, Portuguese and Japanese. Semantic similarity between sentences strongly predicts the similarity of scan patterns in all three languages, even across languages. Syntax had a secondary, brief effect, confined to early planning within language and within scene.
numbers: 74 participants: 24 English, 28 European Portuguese, 20 Japanese (Japanese speakers lived in Portugal about 5.9 months on average). Gaze split into planning and articulation phases.
limits: Small groups; Japanese sample were residents abroad.
agent_relevance: Supports two layers: a shared meaning plan and language-specific linearisation. A scaffold can plan content first and order it later.

source: Papafragou, Hulbert & Trueswell (2008), framing of competing accounts
finding: The paper contrasts three outcomes: language shapes attention always, only when speaking (thinking for speaking), or never even while planning. Data favour the middle outcome. It names Bowerman & Levinson 2001, Gentner & Boroditsky 2001 and Slobin 2003 as stronger accounts that the non-linguistic results are hard to reconcile with.
limits: Written by the study authors, so the framing favours their reading.
agent_relevance: Separate three claims when judging any LLM study: input-language effects, output-planning effects, representation effects.

source: Language of Thought Shapes Output Diversity in Large Language Models (arXiv 2601.11227)
finding: Closest LLM analogue to thinking for speaking: the language a reasoning model thinks in changes the diversity of its English answers. Non-English thinking with English answers raises diversity, more for languages farther from English in thinking space. Mixed-language thinking adds more.
numbers: NoveltyBench Distinct Score (%), English / non-English average / mixed: Qwen3-8B 28.55 / 36.00 / 43.73; Qwen3-14B 26.20 / 31.45 / 38.00; Qwen3-32B 35.00 / 40.30 / 46.53; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B 38.33 / 46.03 / 52.07. Gain 5.3 to 7.7 points; output quality drop 1.02 to 2.24 points; r=0.72 to 0.88 between distance from English and Distinct Score. 15 thinking languages, 100 questions per benchmark.
limits: Authors not confirmed. Small benchmarks (100 questions); Qwen3 and one distill only. Page summary covered the first 100k of 106k characters.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant to our NoveltyBench work: thinking language is a cheap diversity lever at about 1-2 points of quality cost.

source: Language Matters: how do multilingual input and reasoning paths affect large reasoning models? (arXiv 2505.17407)
finding: Reasoning models default to reasoning in a high-resource language (usually English) whatever the input language. Forcing reasoning in the input language lowers reasoning accuracy, most in low-resource languages, but helps some cultural tasks.
numbers: MATH-500 average, English prefill / target-language prefill: Chinese 87.7/85.9, Spanish 88.0/72.5, Russian 86.7/81.6, Swahili 57.4/25.9, Japanese 84.9/66.3, Telugu 70.0/46.2, Korean 83.7/75.4. MMMLU: Swahili 48.8 vs 35.3, Spanish +5.1, Japanese +6.8. Reasoning and answer language mismatched in over 90% of cases for QwQ-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. Cultural benchmark gain +1.0 (South Europe), +2.9 (Oceania).
limits: Four reasoning models. The page showed internal inconsistencies (CulturalBench-Hard size 1,200 vs 4,907 vs 4,709; Spanish 46.8 vs 45.6).
agent_relevance: The model's thinking-for-speaking language is English by default. Scratchpad language is a measurable control with a task-dependent cost or gain.

source: Under the Shadow of Babel: how language shapes reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2506.16151)
finding: Tests linguistic relativity inside models with a Chinese and English causal reasoning dataset (BICAUSE). Models learn language-specific preferences for causal word order and apply them rigidly to reversed order, hurting mainly Chinese.
numbers: 400 samples, 8 domains of 50. Main model Qwen1.5-1.8B-Chat; eight models in total. Accuracy forward 91.0% English, 91.2% Chinese; reversed 88.5% English, 76.5% Chinese (table says 76.8%). SVCCA similarity: En-Zh forward 0.73; English forward vs reversed 0.64; Chinese forward vs reversed about 0.46.
limits: Authors not confirmed. A small model carries the headline numbers; representation similarity is correlated with accuracy, not shown causal.
agent_relevance: Word order learned from training text becomes a bias on reasoning. Argues for giving premises in canonical order.

source: Investigating the influence of prompt and response languages on LLM content generation (arXiv listing 2608.26186)
finding: A search summary said style and lexical choices shift systematically with the instruction language.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Search snippet only; the summary itself flagged the unusual arXiv id. Unverified.
agent_relevance: Lead only.

source: Search note: LLM tests of Slobin-style motion typology
finding: No study was found this session that gives an LLM or vision-language model a motion-event stimulus and measures manner or path verb choice by language. The shared search budget ran out, and Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv search APIs were rate-limited (HTTP 429).
limits: A negative result under tool limits, not proof the literature is empty.
agent_relevance: Possible gap: run Papafragou-style clip descriptions through a multilingual VLM and count manner and path verbs per language.
